title: Intro Psychology: Key Concepts
description: Core ideas from an introductory psychology course, covering learning, memory, the brain, development, social behavior, and research methods.
subject: social-sciences

cards.definition: Learning in which a neutral stimulus becomes linked to a meaningful one and comes to trigger a similar response; studied by Ivan Pavlov with dogs.
Mental discomfort from holding conflicting beliefs or acting against one's beliefs, which pushes people to reduce the conflict.
Tendency for people to be less likely to help someone in need when other people are present.
Learning in which behavior is shaped by its consequences through reinforcement and punishment; associated with B. F. Skinner.
Adding a desirable stimulus after a behavior to make that behavior more likely to happen again.
Removing an unpleasant stimulus after a behavior to make that behavior more likely; it is not the same as punishment.
A consequence that makes a behavior less likely to happen again.
Abraham Maslow's model of human needs, rising from physiological and safety needs through belonging and esteem to self-actualization.
Debate over how much traits and behavior come from genetics versus environment and experience.
Chemical messenger that carries signals across the synapse from one neuron to another.
Brain structure in the temporal lobe that is essential for forming new explicit long-term memories of facts and events.
Almond-shaped brain structure involved in processing emotions, especially fear.
System that briefly holds and manipulates information needed for tasks like reasoning, reading, and problem-solving.
Relatively lasting store of knowledge, skills, and experiences with a very large capacity.
Understanding that objects still exist when they can't be seen; Jean Piaget placed its development in infancy's sensorimotor stage.
Theory, developed by John Bowlby, that early emotional bonds with caregivers shape later social and emotional development.
Adjusting one's behavior or beliefs to match a group; demonstrated in Solomon Asch's line-judgment experiments.
Following direct orders from an authority figure; famously studied in Stanley Milgram's shock experiments.
Improvement in a condition caused by a person's expectations rather than by an active treatment.
Mental shortcut that allows quick judgments and decisions but can sometimes lead to errors.
Sigmund Freud's three parts of personality: instinctual drives, the realistic mediator, and internalized moral standards.
The factor a researcher deliberately changes in an experiment to test its effect.
The outcome a researcher measures in an experiment to see whether the independent variable affected it.
Statistical relationship between two variables; a correlation on its own does not show that one causes the other.
